before.content_html:
Human Sexuality

Human sexuality refers to how people experience and express sexual attraction. People may be heterosexual (attracted to the opposite sex), homosexual (attracted to the same sex), or bisexual (attracted to both sexes). In contemporary British society, all three orientations are widely accepted and protected by law.

Key Fact

Both Christianity and Islam teach that sexual relationships should take place within marriage. However, there is a range of views within Christianity on homosexuality — from conservative opposition to liberal acceptance.

Sexual Relationships Before & Outside Marriage

In modern Britain, sex before marriage is common and widely accepted. However, most religious traditions teach that sexual intimacy belongs within the commitment of marriage.

The Catholic Church teaches that sex must only take place within marriage. St Paul wrote: “Flee from sexual immorality” (1 Corinthians 6:18). Pope Pius XI declared in 1930 that “every sexual act must be within a framework of marriage.” The Church of England generally agrees but is more lenient towards committed couples. Liberal Protestants tend to accept sex in loving, stable relationships even without marriage.

Islam is clear that sex must only happen within marriage. The Qur’an forbids zinah (unlawful sexual intercourse). Under Shari’ah law, sex before marriage is a serious offence. Abdul Wahid Hamid wrote: “The only way to protect all within society is to maintain a society where only a man and his wife share the act of sex.”

Both Christianity and Islam also condemn adultery. The Ten Commandments state: “You shall not commit adultery” (Exodus 20:14). The Qur’an (17:32) warns: “Do not go anywhere near adultery: it is an outrage, and an evil path.”

The Nature & Purpose of Marriage

Marriage is a formal, legal union between two people. For religious believers, it is more than a legal contract — it is a sacred commitment before God. Christians call marriage a sacrament (Catholics and some Anglicans) or a covenant before God.

Key Fact

The purposes of marriage include: lifelong companionship, a stable environment for children, sexual intimacy within a committed relationship, and (for religious believers) following God’s plan. Genesis 2:24 says a man shall “be united to his wife, and they will become one flesh.” The Qur’an (30:21) describes marriage as a source of “love and mercy.”

Same-Sex Marriage & Cohabitation

In a Christian marriage ceremony, couples exchange vows before God, promising to love and cherish each other “for better, for worse, for richer, for poorer, in sickness and in health, till death do us part.” In Islam, the marriage contract is called a nikah. It includes a mahr (financial gift from groom to bride), and both parties must freely consent. The ceremony is often simple, witnessed by family and an imam.

Same-sex marriage became legal in England and Wales in 2013. Many liberal Christians support it, arguing that love and commitment matter more than the gender of the partners. However, the Catholic Church and many evangelical Christians oppose same-sex marriage, teaching that marriage is between a man and a woman as God intended.

Islam does not recognise same-sex marriage. Traditional Islamic teaching holds that marriage can only be between a man and a woman, based on the Qur’an’s teachings about the natural order of creation.

Cohabitation (living together without marriage) is increasingly common in Britain. Most Christians prefer marriage but liberal denominations accept cohabitation in committed relationships. Islam does not accept cohabitation because sexual relationships outside marriage are forbidden.

Divorce & Remarriage

Divorce is the legal ending of a marriage. In Britain, divorce is common — roughly 42% of marriages end in divorce. Religious attitudes vary significantly.

The Catholic Church does not allow divorce because marriage is a sacrament. Jesus taught: “What God has joined together, let no one separate” (Mark 10:9). Catholics may obtain an annulment if the marriage was not valid. The Church of England permits divorce and some clergy will remarry divorced people. Most Protestant churches accept divorce as a last resort, showing compassion for those in unhappy or abusive marriages.

Islam permits divorce but discourages it. The Prophet Muhammad said: “Of all the lawful things, divorce is the most hated by Allah.” There is a waiting period called iddah (three months) to allow time for reconciliation and to check if the wife is pregnant. Both men and women can initiate divorce in Islam, and remarriage is permitted after the iddah period.

Key Fact

The ethical tension around divorce centres on two principles: the sanctity of marriage vows (marriage is sacred and permanent) versus compassion (it is cruel to force people to stay in harmful or loveless marriages). Different religious traditions balance these principles differently.

before.content_html:
The Nature of Families

A family is a group of people connected by blood, marriage or adoption. Families come in many forms in modern Britain. A nuclear family consists of two parents and their children. An extended family includes grandparents, aunts, uncles and cousins. Other family types include single-parent families, blended (step) families, and same-sex parent families.

Both Christianity and Islam place great importance on family life. Families are seen as the foundation of society and the place where children learn right from wrong, receive love and security, and are raised in a faith.

Key Fact

The role of parents is to provide for their children physically, emotionally and spiritually. The role of children is to respect and obey their parents. The Bible says: “Honour your father and your mother” (Exodus 20:12). The Qur’an teaches: “Your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him, and that you be kind to parents” (17:23).

The Purpose of Families

Religious teachings identify several key purposes of family life:

Procreation — Both Christianity and Islam teach that one purpose of marriage and family is to have children. Genesis 1:28 says: “Be fruitful and increase in number.” In Islam, children are seen as a blessing from Allah.

Stability and protection — Families provide a safe, stable environment where children are protected and nurtured. Christians believe the family unit reflects God’s love. Muslims see the family as the building block of the ummah (Muslim community).

Educating children in a faith — Religious families pass on their beliefs and values to the next generation. Christian parents often have children baptised and take them to church. Muslim parents teach children to pray and read the Qur’an from a young age.

Contemporary Family Issues

In modern Britain, same-sex couples can adopt children or have them through surrogacy or IVF. Some Christians accept same-sex parenting, arguing that a loving, stable home is what matters most. Liberal churches emphasise Jesus’s teaching of unconditional love. However, conservative Christians and the Catholic Church oppose same-sex parenting, believing children should be raised by a mother and a father as God intended. Islam does not accept same-sex parenting because homosexual relationships are considered haram (forbidden).

Polygamy means having more than one spouse. It is illegal in the UK. Christianity teaches that marriage is between one man and one woman. However, Islam permits a man to have up to four wives (Qur’an 4:3), provided he treats each wife equally. In practice, most British Muslims are monogamous. The Qur’an itself acknowledges this is difficult: “You will never be able to be equal between wives, even if it is your ardent desire” (4:129).

The Roles of Men & Women

Traditionally, men and women had distinct roles — men as providers and protectors, women as homemakers and carers. Many religious teachings reflect these traditional roles. St Paul wrote: “Wives, submit yourselves to your own husbands” (Ephesians 5:22). In Islam, the Qur’an (4:34) states: “Men are the protectors and maintainers of women.”

Key Fact

However, many modern Christians argue for full equality between men and women. Galatians 3:28 says: “There is neither male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus.” Similarly, the Qur’an (33:35) promises equal spiritual rewards for believing men and women. Many Muslims argue that Islam gave women rights to own property, inherit and divorce centuries before Western law did.

Gender Equality, Prejudice & Discrimination

Gender equality means treating men and women with equal rights and opportunities. Discrimination based on gender is illegal in the UK under the Equality Act 2010.

Examples of gender discrimination in religion include the Catholic Church only allowing men to be priests, and some mosques having separate (sometimes smaller) areas for women. However, many denominations now ordain women — the Church of England has had female priests since 1994 and female bishops since 2015. Many Christians and Muslims actively campaign for gender equality as part of their faith’s commitment to justice.

For equality: Both men and women are created in God’s image (Genesis 1:27). Galatians 3:28 teaches spiritual equality. The Qur’an (33:35) promises equal rewards. Jesus treated women with respect and included them among his followers (e.g. Mary Magdalene).

Against full equality of roles: Some believe God gave men and women different but complementary roles. St Paul said women should not teach or have authority over men (1 Timothy 2:12). In Islam, men are traditionally expected to provide financially while women manage the household, though both roles are valued.

Key Fact

Prejudice means holding unfair opinions about someone based on their gender (or other characteristics). Discrimination is acting on those prejudices. Both Christianity and Islam teach that prejudice is wrong because all people are equal before God.

Contraception & Family Planning

Contraception is the deliberate prevention of pregnancy. In modern Britain, contraception is widely available and accepted as a normal part of family planning. However, religious views on contraception vary significantly.

Key Fact

The Catholic Church is the only major Christian denomination that opposes all artificial contraception. Pope Paul VI’s encyclical Humanae Vitae (1968) taught that every sexual act must be open to the possibility of creating life. Catholics may only use natural family planning (tracking fertility cycles).

Most Protestant denominations, including the Church of England, accept the use of artificial contraception. They argue that responsible family planning allows couples to provide better for the children they do have. The Methodist Church stated that “responsible contraception is a welcome means towards fulfilment in marriage.” Contraception can also help prevent the spread of sexually transmitted infections. Protestants see family planning as a practical way to show love and responsibility.

Islamic views on contraception are divided. Many Muslim scholars accept contraception within marriage, particularly if pregnancy would harm the mother’s health, the family cannot afford more children, or it would protect existing children’s welfare. The Hadith records that some companions of the Prophet practised withdrawal (coitus interruptus) and he did not forbid it. However, some scholars oppose contraception because children are a blessing from Allah and humans should not interfere with God’s will. Methods that are permanent (such as sterilisation) are generally considered haram unless medically necessary.

Sexual Relationships Before Marriage

The specification requires you to explain contrasting beliefs about sexual relationships before marriage. In contemporary British society, pre-marital sex is widely accepted. However, most religious traditions teach that sex should be reserved for marriage.

Christianity: The Catholic Church teaches that sex must only take place within marriage. St Paul wrote: “Flee from sexual immorality” (1 Corinthians 6:18). However, liberal Protestants tend to accept sex within committed, loving relationships even without marriage.

Islam: Sex before marriage is strictly forbidden. The Qur’an prohibits zinah (unlawful sexual intercourse). Under Shari’ah law, sex outside marriage is a serious offence. There is no liberal/conservative divide on this issue in Islam — the teaching is clear and universal.

Same-Sex Relationships

Same-sex relationships are legally protected in the UK. The Equality Act 2010 makes discrimination based on sexual orientation illegal. Same-sex marriage has been legal in England and Wales since 2013. However, religious views on same-sex relationships vary widely.

Key Fact

AQA requires you to explain contrasting beliefs on same-sex relationships with reference to Christianity and at least one other religion. Christianity has a wide range of views, from strong opposition to full acceptance. Islam is more uniformly opposed to same-sex relationships.

Christian Views on Same-Sex Relationships

Conservative Christians oppose same-sex relationships. They cite Leviticus 18:22: “Do not have sexual relations with a man as one does with a woman; that is detestable.” The Catholic Church teaches that homosexual orientation is not sinful, but homosexual acts are. The Catechism states that homosexual people “must be accepted with respect, compassion, and sensitivity” but should remain chaste.

Liberal Christians support same-sex relationships. They argue that the Bible must be interpreted in its historical context. Jesus never spoke about homosexuality but taught love for all people. Some denominations, such as the Quakers and United Reformed Church, perform same-sex marriages. They point to Jesus’s commandment: “Love your neighbour as yourself” (Mark 12:31).

The Church of England occupies a middle ground. It welcomes homosexual people and recognises civil partnerships and same-sex marriages performed in civil ceremonies. However, it does not currently allow same-sex marriages to take place in its churches. In 2023, the Church of England voted to allow blessings for same-sex couples but stopped short of allowing full church weddings. This ongoing debate shows how religious organisations can evolve on social issues.

Islamic Views on Same-Sex Relationships

Traditional Islamic teaching opposes all same-sex relationships. The Qur’an (7:80–81) tells the story of the Prophet Lut (Lot), whose people were punished for homosexual behaviour. Homosexual acts are classified as zinah under Shari’ah law.

However, some progressive Muslim organisations in Britain argue for greater acceptance. Groups like the Inclusive Mosque Initiative welcome LGBTQ+ Muslims. Many British Muslims also acknowledge that while they may personally disagree with homosexuality on religious grounds, they respect the laws of the country they live in and oppose discrimination against anyone.

Humanists and atheists generally support same-sex relationships and full equality for LGBTQ+ people. They argue that moral decisions should be based on human rights, happiness and the harm principle — not on ancient religious texts. Since same-sex relationships between consenting adults cause no harm, there is no ethical reason to oppose them. The British Humanist Association actively campaigns for LGBTQ+ rights.

Key Fact

The three contrasting beliefs on same-sex relationships required by AQA are: (1) conservative Christians oppose them (Leviticus 18:22), (2) liberal Christians accept them (love is most important), and (3) Islam opposes them (Qur’an 7:80–81, story of Lut). You must be able to explain why each group holds its view.

before.content_html:
The Nature of Families

A family is a group of people who are related by blood, marriage or adoption. In the 21st century, families come in many different forms. Both Christianity and Islam teach that the family is the foundation of a stable society, but they recognise that families look very different today compared to the past.

Key Fact

You are expected to know six types of family: nuclear, extended, single-parent, blended (step), same-sex parent, and polygamous. You must also understand the purpose of families and contemporary issues such as same-sex parenting and polygamy.

Types of Family

There are several types of family that you need to know for the exam. Each has a clear definition that the exam board uses.

A nuclear family is a couple and their children living together as a basic social unit. An extended family goes beyond this by including grandparents, aunts, uncles and other relatives. A single-parent family is one parent raising their children alone, perhaps due to bereavement or the end of a relationship. A blended family (also called a stepfamily) is formed when a divorced or widowed person remarries and brings children from a previous relationship. Same-sex parents are two people of the same gender raising children together, often through adoption or surrogacy. Polygamy is the practice of having more than one spouse at the same time.

The Purpose of Families

Both religious and non-religious people agree that the family serves important purposes in society. Families provide stability, protection and education for children. For religious believers, the family also has a spiritual purpose.

Key Fact

The four key purposes of families on The spec are: procreation, stability and the protection of children, and educating children in a faith.

Procreation means having children. For religious believers, this fulfils God’s command to “be fruitful and increase in number” (Genesis 1:28). The family is seen as the proper place for children to be born and raised.

Families create stability for their members and for society as a whole. They protect children by supplying their basic needs and safeguarding them from harm. The Church of England states: “The family remains the most important grouping human beings have ever developed. Children thrive, grow and develop within love and safeguarding of a family.”

For religious parents, educating children in their faith is a key purpose of family life. Christian parents may baptise their children as a way of committing to raising them in the Christian faith. Muslim parents are expected to teach their children how to pray, keep halal food laws and live according to Islam.

Christian Beliefs About Families

Christians believe the family reflects the family of God and provides the basis for a stable society. Parents have a responsibility to care for their children and raise them in the faith. The Bible teaches: “Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right. ‘Honour your father and mother’” (Ephesians 6:1–2). Parents also have duties: “Fathers, do not embitter your children, or they will become discouraged” (Colossians 3:21).

The Bible emphasises providing for your family: “Anyone who does not provide for their relatives, and especially for their own household, has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Timothy 5:8). Children are described as “a heritage from the Lord, offspring a reward from him” (Psalm 127:3).

Islamic Beliefs About Families

In Islam, the extended family is the basis of Islamic society and part of God’s plan for human beings. The family shapes the moral values and character of children. The Qur’an teaches respect for parents: “Your Lord has commanded that you should worship none but Him, and that you be kind to your parents” (Qur’an 17:23).

The Hadith teaches that “Heaven is under the feet of the mothers,” showing the high status given to mothers in Islam. Children have a duty to care for their elderly parents with kindness and respect. Muslim parents are expected to love and care for their children, set a good example for them, and bring them up in the faith of Islam. The Hadith states: “Honour your children and perfect their manners.”

In Christianity, parents look after their children, caring for them and teaching them about the faith. Children obey their parents and may look after them when they are old. In Islam, men are traditionally expected to provide for the family while women look after the home and raise the children, though many modern British Muslim families share these duties. Children must show respect and care for their parents in old age — the Qur’an instructs: “Lower your wing in humility towards your parents in kindness” (Qur’an 17:24).

Contemporary Family Issues

Modern society raises several issues about family life that religious believers must respond to.

Key Fact

Same-sex adoption is legal in the UK. Polygamy is not legal in the UK, but polygamous marriages performed outside the UK may be recognised.

If a same-sex couple wish to have children, they will generally adopt or have a child biologically related to one parent through surrogacy or sperm donation. Some traditional Christians disapprove of same-sex parents because they believe the ideal is for children to grow up with a male and female role model. Other Christians say it is more important for children to be in a secure and loving family regardless of the gender of their parents. Muslims generally do not approve of same-sex parenting because Islam considers homosexuality morally wrong and believes children should have both a male and female role model.

Bigamy (marrying someone while still married to another) is a criminal offence in the UK. Polygamy may mean that children have the support of more parent figures, but it can also cause jealousy among spouses and mean children see their parents less if a father has multiple households. Christians generally oppose polygamy, though it is not expressly forbidden in the Bible. In Islam, polygamy is permitted under Shari’ah law — a man may marry up to four wives, provided he treats them all equally. However, many Muslims in Britain do not practise polygamy.

Award up to 4 marks, 2 per contrasting belief.
Possible answers:
• Some Christians say it is more important for children to be in a secure and loving family regardless of the gender of their parents. They believe love is the most important factor in raising children (2 marks).
• Muslims generally do not approve of same-sex parenting because Islam considers homosexuality morally wrong and believes children need both a male and female role model as parents (2 marks).

This shows that failing to look after your family goes against the Christian faith (developed point + scripture = 3 marks).
• Muslims believe parents should raise their children in the faith of Islam, teaching them to pray and live a good Muslim life. The Hadith teaches: ‘Honour your children and perfect their manners.’ This shows that parents have a duty to set a moral example (developed point + scripture = 2 marks).

Points FOR:

• Same-sex couples adopting can give children without parents a good, loving home.

Points AGAINST:

• Muslims believe homosexuality is morally wrong, so same-sex parents cannot set a good moral example to their children according to Islamic teachings.
• The Bible implies marriage and family should be between a man and a woman: ‘God made them male and female’ (Mark 10:6).

before.content_html:
Gender Equality in Britain Today

Gender equality means that men and women should be given the same rights and opportunities as each other. Many people in Britain today agree with the idea of gender equality, but there are still many examples where it does not happen. Something that prevents gender equality is gender prejudice, which is often based on sexual stereotyping.

An example of sexual stereotyping is the idea that women are more naturally caring or are the weaker sex, so they should look after the home while men go out to work. Stereotyping can lead to gender discrimination — perhaps by not giving a man a job looking after young children or not employing a woman on a building site.

Key Fact

The Sex Discrimination Act (1975) made gender discrimination illegal in the UK. Despite this, it still occurs — on average women get paid less than men, even when doing the same jobs. Women make up roughly half of the workforce, but men hold a higher proportion of senior positions.

Christian Views on Gender Equality

Christians believe that all people have been created as equals in the image of God. The Bible teaches that men and women are equal in God’s sight: “There is neither Jew nor Gentile, neither slave nor free, nor is there male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 3:28). God created both male and female in his image: “So God created humankind in his image, in the image of God he created them; male and female he created them” (Genesis 1:27).

Jesus treated women with respect, welcomed them as disciples, and showed in the story of Mary and Martha that women were capable of things other than domestic tasks. He did not conform to the status quo of his day. Christians have worked with charities to improve the treatment of women worldwide and campaigned for more equal treatment of women and men politically.

Some Christians believe that husbands should be in charge of their wives because of biblical teaching: “Wives, be subject to your husbands as you are to the Lord. For the husband is the head of the wife just as Christ is the head of the church” (Ephesians 5:22–23). St Paul also wrote: “I permit no woman to teach or to have authority over a man” (1 Timothy 2:12).

Some Christians feel that women should focus on motherhood, because important Christian figures such as Mary are revered because they were mothers. The command “with painful labour you will give birth to children. Your desire will be for your husband, and he will rule over you” (Genesis 3:16) is also cited, though many see this as reflecting punishment for disobedience rather than God’s original plan.

Key Fact

Most Christians today see marriage as an equal partnership where the different gifts of each person, male and female, strengthen family life. Many Christians also argue that inflammatory Bible and Church teachings about gender roles could be considered out of date, reflecting the position of women at the time the Bible was written rather than God’s will for today.

Women in Christian Leadership

The question of whether women can hold leadership roles in the Church is one of the most visible areas of debate about gender equality in Christianity. Some Christians, particularly Catholics, feel that women should not be ordained as priests because of biblical teaching, because Jesus and his disciples were male, and because it is a long-standing tradition in the Catholic Church.

However, other Christians see this as unfair discrimination. Many churches allow women to become vicars and ministers. The Church of England has allowed women to become bishops since 2014. These Christians argue that if God created men and women as equals, then both should be able to serve in all roles within the Church.

Muslim Views on Gender Equality

Muslims believe that God created all people equal. The Qur’an teaches that men and women were created from a single soul and have the same spiritual nature. Men and women have the same religious and moral responsibilities. Muhammad worked to unite tribes in Madinah into one community (Ummah) under God, with equality and justice for all.

The Qur’an states: “People, We created you all from a single man and a single woman, and made you into races and tribes so that you could recognise one another” (Qur’an 49:13). Muhammad also taught that anyone, man or woman, who does a good deed for God’s sake will be rewarded (Qur’an 16:97). He said: “I command you to be kind to women.”

Many Muslim families place high value on the mother’s role in bringing up children in Islam. Men are expected to provide for their families and make decisions about their general welfare. However, many modern British Muslim families share those duties because often both parents have jobs.

Islamic law recognises the full property rights of women before and after marriage. A married woman may keep her maiden name and is entitled to receive material gifts. She does not need to spend her own money on the household and has the right to full financial support within marriage and during the waiting period of divorce.

Key Fact

In some Muslim countries, women are not given full rights under the law, but Muslims point out this is due to different cultural practices rather than the teachings of the Qur’an. Muslim women in the UK may suffer prejudice for the way they dress, for example wearing the hijab. Research shows Muslim women are 71% more likely to be unemployed than white Christian women with the same education level and language skills.

Challenging Gender Prejudice and Discrimination

Christians who think men and women should have different roles may still see them as equal. They may think it is fair to treat them in different ways if this is God’s will. However, Christians who disagree with different gender roles may see men and women being given different roles as unequal treatment, and they may view this as prejudice and discrimination.

Most Christians think it is wrong to treat people differently in any unfair way because they believe God loves everyone equally. The command to “love one’s neighbour” means that to discriminate is not loving. Many non-religious people also agree that men and women should be treated equally. Humanist principles such as fairness and equal rights support this view. Gender prejudice and discrimination is illegal in the UK.

Many non-religious people agree that men and women should be treated equally, and that gender prejudice and discrimination are wrong. Humanist principles of fairness and equal rights support this. However, some non-religious people may believe men and women should have different roles due to biological differences, or may be influenced by social and cultural standards or personal prejudices.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Gender equality means giving people the same rights regardless of gender. The Sex Discrimination Act (1975) made gender discrimination illegal in the UK, but inequalities persist in areas like pay and senior positions.
  • Both Christianity and Islam teach that men and women are equal before God, but there are different views within each religion about whether men and women should have the same or different roles.
  • The debate over women’s ordination in Christianity (e.g. Catholic priests vs Church of England bishops since 2014) is a key example of how gender equality is applied differently within religions.

In your answer you should refer to the main religious tradition of Great Britain and one or more other religious traditions.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• Some Christians (such as Catholics) believe women should not be ordained as priests because Jesus and his disciples were male, and it is a tradition in the Catholic Church (1 mark for belief, 1 mark for development/reasoning).
• In Islam, men and women are considered spiritually equal — the Qur’an teaches that men and women were created from a single soul and have the same religious and moral responsibilities. However, men are expected to provide for the family (1 mark for belief, 1 mark for development/reasoning).
Accept other valid contrasting responses that reference Christianity and at least one other tradition.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two religious beliefs about gender equality.
Refer to scripture or sacred writings in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Marking: First belief (1–2 marks) + Second belief (1–2 marks) + Source of authority named and applied (1–2 marks) = up to 6 marks.

Award up to 6 marks:
• One belief: Christians believe men and women are equal in God’s sight because the Bible says “There is neither Jew nor Gentile, neither slave nor free, nor is there male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 3:28). This means that in God’s eyes, gender does not determine a person’s worth (up to 3 marks: 1 for belief, 1 for source, 1 for development).
• Second belief: Muslims believe God created all people equal — the Qur’an teaches “People, We created you all from a single man and a single woman” (Qur’an 49:13). This shows that men and women share the same origin and spiritual nature (up to 2 marks: 1 for belief with source, 1 for development).
Accept other valid beliefs supported by relevant scripture.

practice_questions.text:
'Women can never be equal to men.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you:
• should give reasoned arguments in support of this statement
• should give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• should refer to religious arguments
• may refer to non-religious arguments
• should reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Some Christians argue men and women have different roles given by God — “Wives, be subject to your husbands” (Ephesians 5:22) and “I permit no woman to teach or to have authority over a man” (1 Timothy 2:12)
• Catholic Church does not allow women to become priests, seeing it as tradition based on Jesus choosing male disciples
• In many Muslim families, men are expected to be the providers and decision-makers for the household
• Biologically, men and women are different, which some argue leads to naturally different roles
Arguments against:
• Galatians 3:28 teaches there is no male or female in Christ — all are equal before God
• The Qur’an teaches men and women were created from a single soul (49:13) with equal spiritual worth
• Jesus treated women with respect and as equals, challenging the norms of his time
• The Sex Discrimination Act (1975) made gender discrimination illegal, reflecting society’s view that equality is a right
• Church of England has allowed women bishops since 2014
• Having different roles does not necessarily mean being unequal
Conclusion should follow logically from arguments made.
Top band (10-12): A well-argued response with religious and/or non-religious arguments on both sides, clear references to teachings, and a justified conclusion.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Clear arguments on both sides with some religious references.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Some arguments given, limited development or one-sided.
Lower band (1-3): Simple or limited points made.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two religious beliefs about the roles of men and women.
Refer to scripture or sacred writings in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Marking: First belief (1–2 marks) + Second belief (1–2 marks) + Source of authority named and applied (1–2 marks) = up to 6 marks.

Award up to 6 marks:
• One belief: Some Christians believe that men should lead in the family because St Paul wrote “the husband is the head of the wife just as Christ is the head of the church” (Ephesians 5:23). This means that the man has a responsibility to care for and guide his family, as Christ cares for the Church (up to 3 marks: 1 for belief, 1 for source, 1 for development).
• Second belief: In Islam, the Qur’an teaches that men and women have complementary roles — “People, We created you all from a single man and a single woman” (Qur’an 49:13). This means both are valued equally by God, even if they may take on different responsibilities within the family (up to 2 marks: 1 for belief with source, 1 for development).
Accept other valid beliefs supported by relevant scripture.

flashcard_questions.q: Giving people the same rights and opportunities regardless of whether they are male or female.
Unfairly judging someone before the facts are known; holding biased opinions about an individual or group based on their gender.
Having a fixed general idea or image of how men and women will behave.
_____ Equality in Britain Today Gender equality means that men and women should be given the same rights and opportunities as each other
